role: Local test of the bwx12 kernel source and its acceptance checker. It measures nothing.
purpose: This script tests the source of the runner bwx12 on the development machine (x86-64) and prints one PASS or FAIL line per check. It measures no rate and assembles no AArch64 code, so it does not prove what machine code ran on CRB.

main_flow.step: A person or an AI agent starts the script on the development machine, with no argument: `python3 test_kernels12.py`. With `KEEP=1` in the environment the temporary folder is kept.
The script finds its own folder and the folder `ref-bwx11`, and loads `check_listing12.py` as the module `cl`.
`main` creates a temporary folder. The builds and the listings of the test are written there.
Step 1, `test_source` (2 checks): `bwx12.c` and `bwx12_selftest.c` without their marked additions must have the sha256 of the accepted `bwx11.c` and `bwx11_selftest.c`.

Step 2, `test_standin` (6 checks): `build12.sh` builds the program with and without the 26 new kernels, as x86-64 code with stand-in kernels. Both builds must succeed. `--list` must print 55 names. The self-test must report no failure, with the expected number of passed rows per new kernel. The 29 old kernels must have the same machine code and the same loop offset in both builds. The functions `call` to `timed_sequence_hot` must start at the same address modulo 64 in both builds.

Step 3, first part of `test_aarch64_text` (3 checks): the asm text of the 26 new kernels is taken from the output of `gcc -E -D__aarch64__` and written as a listing. The listing must pass the checker. Every vector register of the text must be in the clobber list.
Step 4, second part of `test_aarch64_text` (7 checks): 7 changed copies of that listing must fail in the checker, each on the changed kernel only.
`main` deletes the temporary folder if `KEEP` is not set. It prints `# failed checks: N`. The exit status is 1 if a check failed and 0 if not.

behavior_notes: How it is run: a person or an AI agent starts it with a command on the development machine. It is made for that machine, not for CRB. No script of the whole-chip test (`go.sh`, `go2.sh`, `ra.sh`, `rx.sh`) calls it. It times nothing and prints no rate.

Names: in this file "new kernels" are the 26 kernels of round 5 and "old kernels" are the 29 kernels of bwx11. Of bwx12, the whole-chip test runs `oldread`, `read`, `asmread`, `read_nop96`, `read_nop256` and `read_1pl`. Of these, only `read_nop256` is a new kernel in the sense of this file. The other five are among the 29 old kernels.

A full run prints 18 check lines and the line `# failed checks: N`. It prints fewer check lines when a build fails (lines 99-100). It also prints fewer when `aarch64_functions` stops with an error (lines 215-217): gcc fails, a kernel is not found in the gcc output, or an asm text does not end with `b.lo 1b`. Any other error in a test function ends the script with a Python traceback and exit status 1. The line `# failed checks: N` is then not printed.

What a pass of step 1 proves: every line of `bwx12.c` and `bwx12_selftest.c` outside the marked blocks is the accepted bwx11 text, byte for byte. This covers the source of the five old kernels that the whole-chip test runs. It also covers `worker` and `call`, the functions that time and call the kernels in every bwx12 process of the whole-chip test [Ref3].

What a pass of step 2 proves: in an x86-64 build with stand-in kernels, the additions change neither the instruction text nor the loop offset of the 29 old kernels. They also do not change the start modulo 64 of `call`, `read_smaps`, `tcount`, `timed_sequence` and `timed_sequence_hot`. This step proves nothing about AArch64 code.

What a pass of step 3 proves: the asm text of each new kernel, after the expansion of macros and of `.rept`, is the instruction list that the checker expects. For `read_nop256` that is 8 `ldp`, 256 `nop`, `add`, `cmp` and the loop branch. One pass of this loop reads 256 B and uses no loaded value. The pads of the source give the planned loop offsets of 20 B, 40 B and 52 B, if gcc makes the assumed frame.
What a pass of step 4 proves: the checker rejects 7 wrong listings and reports only the changed kernel. One of them is `read_nop256` with 255 `nop`.

What the test does not prove: it assembles no AArch64 code. The test writes these parts itself, and no compiler made them: the frame (`FRAME`, `UNFRAME`), the end-pointer instruction, the `ret`, and the registers x0, x1 and x2. The evidence for the binary that ran on CRB is the checker result on the listing of the CRB build: 29 old kernels and 26 new kernels, 0 failed rows [Ref5]. The script `go.sh` of the whole-chip test stops before the first measurement when the binary `bwx12` does not have the sha256 of that build [Ref10].

The old read kernel and the new read kernel: steps 3 and 4 look only at the 26 new kernels. So no step of this test checks AArch64 machine code of `oldread` or `read`. The test also does not read the binaries bw_old and bw_new of part A.

Check made for this page on 2026-11-21, not by the test. `synth` wrote the 26 blocks with the start address 0x5c80, the address of the first new kernel in the CRB build. These blocks were compared with the 26 blocks of the listing of the CRB build. Every address and every instruction is equal, and the 26 rows of the offsets table are equal. So gcc made the assumed frame on CRB [Ref6].

The local file `bwx12.c` has the sha256 `e3d4442b83d0aabdb8bf68ec62dfeb43d489df1d7c36de82e64e5482a1089127`. The build record of the CRB build lists the same value [Ref6]. So the text that this test reads is the text that was built on CRB.

Run on record: on 2026-11-15 at 17:11:57 UTC an AI agent (Claude Code) ran the whole test on the development machine. The run printed 18 PASS lines and `# failed checks: 0`. The saved record of the agent's commands holds the command and the output [Ref11]. In the same record, a later command of 17:12:10 UTC copies the sources to CRB and starts `build12.sh` there. So the test passed before the CRB build. The record lies outside the project folder. The project folder holds no saved output of the test.

The run on record used the present files. The evidence is the modification times: the test file and the seven files that it reads from its own folder were last written between 17:05:03 UTC and 17:08:48 UTC on 2026-11-15.

For this page, `test_source` and `test_aarch64_text` were called on 2026-11-21 in a temporary work folder (gcc 11.4.0, x86-64). They printed 2 and 10 PASS lines and no FAIL line. `test_standin` was not called. It runs `build12.sh` and the built binary, and the rules of this task forbid that.

Programs that the test starts: `build12.sh` 2 times, the binary of the folder `new` with `--list` 1 time, `gcc -E` 1 time, and `check_listing12.py` 9 times. Each run of `build12.sh` starts gcc, the built binary with `--selftest` and with `--list`, `objdump`, `nm` (a tool that lists the symbols of a binary) and small text tools [Ref4]. The builds work on copies in the temporary folder.

words.def: the Arm reference server under test. It has 128 CPUs.
the run of 2026-11-17 on the whole chip. Of bwx12 it ran six kernels: `oldread`, `read`, `asmread`, `read_nop96`, `read_nop256` and `read_1pl`.
the run of `build12.sh` on CRB on 2026-11-15 that built the binary `bwx12` of the whole-chip test [Ref10]. The folder `crb-build-1` beside this script holds its records, without the binary [Ref6].
our runs use CPUs 0-119 only: 64 threads on mesh 0 plus 56 threads on mesh 1. Each thread reads its own buffer of 256 MiB from memory.
the two halves of the chip. CPUs 0-63 sit on mesh 0. CPUs 64-127 sit on mesh 1.
the x86-64 machine on which this test runs. It has no compiler for AArch64.

an AI agent is an AI coding assistant (Claude Code) that worked on this project for the user. Claude Code saves each command of an agent, with its time and its output, in a record file with one JSON record per line.
the 64-bit instruction set of Arm CPUs. CRB uses it.
with the option `-E`, gcc runs only its preprocessor. It expands macros and includes, and it compiles nothing. With `-D__aarch64__` the output holds the AArch64 branch of the source.
the inner loop of the benchmark that reads memory. On this page "kernel" means this loop. The operating system kernel is always written "Linux kernel".
loops of the same benchmark that write memory or copy it. In `bwx12.c` the function of a kernel is named `k_<name>`.
portable C code with 16 running sums. Each load is followed by an add. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_old and `oldread` in the runner bwx12.
NEON intrinsics (C functions that map to Arm vector instructions), loads only. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_new and `read` in bwx12.
the benchmark and its two binaries of 2026-11-13. bw_old was built from the old source, bw_new from the new source.
later runner programs for the same loops. They print one row per thread. bwx12 is the runner of the 2026-11-15 investigation. bwx11 and bwx are older versions.
a hand-written load-only loop. It has the same 8 "ldp q" loads per 256 B as the new read kernel. "ldp q" is the Arm instruction that loads two 16-byte vector registers.

two of the 29 old kernels. They are hand-written loops, like asmread. Per 256 B, asmwrite has 8 "stp q" stores, and asmcopy has 8 "ldp q" loads and 8 "stp q" stores [Ref8]. "stp q" is the Arm instruction that stores two 16-byte vector registers.
test loops of bwx12: the asmread loop with 96 or 256 no-operation instructions per 256 B, and a loop with one load per 64 B line.

a process is one start of a benchmark binary. An interval is one timed measurement inside a process. bwx12 times a sequence of kernels and repeats the sequence: each repeat is a round (counted from 0), and the position is the place of a kernel in the sequence (counted from 0). In part A the round (1 or 2) is the round of the script: round 2 runs the processes in the reverse order.
the 120-thread part of the test of 2026-11-13, repeated with the same two binaries.
one bwx12 process with the kernel sequence oldread, asmread, read_nop96, read_nop256, read_1pl.

the two modes of bwx12. Interval mode (option `--seq`): each thread runs a sequence of kernels, and the function `worker` times each kernel in one interval. The whole-chip test uses it. Trial mode (option `--trial`): the functions `timed_sequence` and `timed_sequence_hot` call and time the kernels. The whole-chip test does not use it.

two more functions of `bwx12.c` [Ref3]. `read_smaps` reads from the Linux file `/proc/self/smaps` how many kB of a buffer lie on 2 MiB pages (transparent huge pages). `tcount` reads the event counters and the CPU time of the thread in the trial mode.
in this file: the name that the source gives to its additions of 2026-11-15. `bwx12.c` is `bwx11.c` plus these additions. It is not a round of a measurement.

words.term: New kernels, old kernels (in this file)
words.def: the new kernels are the 26 kernels that round 5 added: 9 `read_nop`, 4 `read_dadd`, `read_iadd16`, 5 `read_sp`, `read_1pl_nop96`, 4 `write_nop`, 2 `copy_nop`. The old kernels are the 29 kernels that bwx11 already had. These words do not mean the new read kernel and the old read kernel.
the build of bwx11 that the checker uses as its reference. The folder `ref-bwx11` beside the script holds its build record (`build.txt`), its listing and its offsets table.

two ways in which `bwx12.c` writes a kernel for AArch64. A NEON kernel is C code with NEON intrinsics (C functions that map to Arm vector instructions). An asm kernel is assembler text inside a gcc `__asm__` statement.
a plain C loop that replaces a NEON or asm kernel when `bwx12.c` is compiled on a machine that is not AArch64. It touches the same bytes as the real kernel. Rates of a stand-in build mean nothing.
the run `bwx12 --selftest`. The binary runs every kernel on small buffers and prints one row per check: kernel, check, bytes, `pass` or `FAIL`.
the build script of bwx12. It compiles `bwx12.c`, runs the self-test, and writes `build.txt`, `listing.txt` and `offsets.tsv` into its own folder.
a Linux tool that starts a program limited to a list of CPUs.
by default `/tmp/positron-perf.RUNNING`. Another user creates it during a performance test. `build12.sh` and the run scripts of the whole-chip test stop when this file exists.

the acceptance test of a bwx12 build. It compares a listing and an offsets table with the accepted bwx11 build and with the expected loop of each new kernel. Exit status 0: all rules passed. Exit status 1: a rule failed. Exit status 2: a file could not be used.

`objdump` is a tool that prints the machine code of a binary as instruction text. The listing (`listing.txt`) holds one block per kernel: a title line `=== bwx12 <kernel> ===`, then one line per instruction with its address.
the file `offsets.tsv`. One row per kernel: binary, kernel, function, start address, loop start address, loop start modulo 64.

the address of the first instruction of the loop, modulo 64. The value is a number of bytes from 0 to 63. The plan is 20 B for a read kernel, 40 B for a write kernel and 52 B for a copy kernel of round 5.
`PLACE(name)` is a macro of `bwx12.c` that stands directly before a kernel. It fills the code up to a 64 B boundary and then adds `pad` zero bytes. So the function starts at `pad` modulo 64.
parts of a gcc `__asm__` statement. The template is the assembler text, written as string literals. The clobber list names the registers that the text changes.
assembler syntax in the asm text. The lines between `.rept N` and `.endr` are repeated N times. `1:` is a label. `b.lo 1b` branches back to the label `1:` that stands before it.
here: the instructions that the compiler adds before and after the asm text of a kernel. They store the registers d8 to d15 to the stack before the loop and load them back after it.

the instruction before the loop that computes the address at which the loop stops. For a read or write kernel it is `add x1, x0, x1, lsl #3`: end = start + 8 B per 64-bit word. The compiler makes it from a C statement of the kernel function. It is not part of the asm text.
AArch64 has 32 vector registers, v0 to v31. q8 names the 16 bytes of v8, and d8 names its low 8 bytes. A function must return d8 to d15 unchanged to its caller.

words.term: ldp, stp, nop, movi, dup, b.lo
words.def: Arm instructions. `ldp` loads two registers and `stp` stores two registers. `nop` does nothing. `movi` sets a vector register to a constant. `dup` copies a general register into each element of a vector register. `b.lo` branches when the compare found "lower". `objdump` prints it as `b.cc`.
a checksum of 64 hexadecimal digits. Two files with the same sha256 are taken as equal, byte for byte.

functions.name: check
functions.what: Prints one PASS or FAIL line for a check and counts the failed checks in `fails`.

functions.name: strip12
functions.what: Returns a source text without the blocks between the marker lines `bwx12+` and `bwx12-`.

functions.name: run
functions.what: Starts a command, waits for it, and returns exit status, standard output and error output.

functions.name: test_source
functions.what: Step 1: compares the sha256 of the bwx12 sources without their additions with the accepted bwx11 values.

functions.name: test_standin
functions.what: Step 2: builds the program with and without the new kernels on x86-64 and compares the 29 old kernels.

functions.name: aarch64_functions
functions.what: Runs `gcc -E -D__aarch64__` and returns pad, instruction lists and operand text of each new kernel.

functions.name: spell
functions.what: Inner function: writes the number of an `add` or `movi` in hexadecimal, as objdump prints it.

functions.name: synth
functions.what: Writes the listing text and the offsets rows of the 26 new kernels, with an optional change.

functions.name: test_aarch64_text
functions.what: Steps 3 and 4: the listing made from the asm text must pass the checker, and 7 changed copies must fail.

functions.name: result
functions.what: Inner function: writes the accepted bwx11 listing plus the 26 blocks to files and runs the checker on them.

functions.name: one_nop_less
functions.what: Returns a change function that removes one `nop` from the loop of one kernel.

functions.name: other_source
functions.what: Change: one add of `read_dadd8` takes v24 in place of the loaded register v2.

functions.name: no_d8
functions.what: Change: `read_iadd16` does not store d8 and d9.

functions.name: no_init
functions.what: Change: `read_dadd2` lacks the `movi` of v16, and the loop keeps its address.

functions.name: main
functions.what: Creates the temporary folder, runs the three test functions, cleans up, and returns 1 if a check failed.
